name: Hana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach beginner saxophone on Tuesdays, play with a community band at festivals and record simple parts when someone calls. I finished secondary school and am still learning from the older players, especially when the tempo moves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what is tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a child find a note and hearing the town band sound full. Chasing a festival payment while the mortgage and the children’s school letters arrive is tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the community band that AI fixing our rehearsal notices saves me a phone call. I still need to practise my saxophone part before I stand beside the better players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have around four months of expenses saved, and my partner’s school office pay covers the mortgage with mine. I still notice that a missed festival fee means less for the children’s trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep Tuesday beginner sax lessons and the weekend band rehearsals this term. I already use AI daily to draft practice sheets, and I will keep checking the fingerings before pupils see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about festival bookings but secure enough for the next few months. A cleaner notice is welcome, not a reason to change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the festival shortened your set?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the festival moved us to a shorter set and paid the agreed fee. I would ask for the same written terms next season before putting that money toward the children’s trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your children see you learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school after secondary school and learned the sax part slowly. Practice counts even when a tool makes the page look tidy.

I would say **practice together** still makes the concert.

A lost **festival fee** would trim family trips, not this month’s mortgage.

Check current **AI practice sheets** for fingerings before giving them to pupils.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about bookings while household income remains steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band committee that AI may write parts, schedule players and answer bookers, and we should ask which fees are still paid. I would want the musicians association in that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small recording parts I sell might disappear, and festivals may hire fewer players. Four months saved gives us time, but the children’s trips and mortgage still depend on work coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring three festival contracts to the association meeting and ask the booker for a paid-date list. In the first year I would trial an AI range checker on one sax part only after a trusted bandmate shows it working, then play the line myself before sharing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own recording income. The association gives me people to ask, but it cannot guarantee a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep out of a new AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload pupil names or recordings to an unknown service. If the association approves a tool, I would still use a score without names for the first test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How large is the festival fee to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The festival fee is about a sixth of my good-month income. If that went, I would postpone the children’s trip, not pretend the mortgage had become optional.

I would bring the **musicians association** into the fee discussion.

The **festival fee** funds family plans and a slice of monthly income.

feel: I feel **anxious** about recording fees, with people to help me ask questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the community band that AGI by 2028 could write every part, but it should not decide a player’s worth by a cheap file. I would ask for a written festival roster before rehearsals start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the recording parts to disappear in 2028, and some festival dates may be cut before robots can play live around 2031. My partner’s pay and four months saved give us time, but my own lost fees would still need replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would collect my recording invoices and ask the association about wage help for musicians whose paid dates disappear. If 2028 AGI cuts festival dates, I would apply for an open school music aide post only if it accepts my secondary school education and fits child pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious. I expect to lose part of my income, but I can search while the mortgage is covered for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you qualified for the school aide opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school advert says music experience may count, but I need to check whether it demands a certificate. I would not quit my pupils for a post I cannot qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner which fees I expect to lose and agree on a minimum savings line of two months. We would cut the trip before drawing the account below that line.

I would defend **paid players** despite cheap machine parts.

fieldNote: Her **2028 recording loss** precedes any 2031 robot effect on live festivals.
The school move requires **qualification and pickup**, with a real vacancy and pupils kept during applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to teach more young players and protect live festivals. I would ask the association to train us for paid school work, not just hold meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording parts probably end in 2031, but I might have paid group teaching by then. Robots around 2034 may play a stage, though I do not know if a town festival would pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the community school to fund two supervised group-teaching observations if the hours fit pickup. If I can manage six pupils afterward, I would take a paid beginner group; in the first year after 2031 I would keep it only while the school pays preparation and a staff teacher stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until that teaching income is real. Five years helps. A planned class cannot pay this week’s mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to handle six pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need a senior teacher to tell me when six children are not listening. I would not take a class alone before I have been observed and approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What payment would make the class worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school to write the preparation hours into the offer. A room full of children without paid time to plan is not a second wage.

say: I would ask for **paid school training** before leading a group.
I would tell the band to protect **live festivals** through 2031.
think: My **recording work** likely ends in 2031 before 2034 stage robots.
A **paid school group** could replace part of that income if approved.
do: Request two **funded observations** this autumn if pickup and staff supervision work.

feel: I feel **anxious** until a real paid class replaces the recording fees.
S3.quote: A planned class cannot pay this week’s mortgage.
fieldNote: Her group route requires **funded observation** and a teacher’s approval before she leads six pupils.
The post-2031 class requires **paid preparation**, staff presence and child pickup that still works.

steps.text: Observe senior teacher twice if school funds hours and pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to learn and to ask for fair pay. I would keep playing festivals that hire real musicians and teach pupils who want to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 school group pay might carry more of the mortgage than festivals. Robots around 2039 could copy a sax part, but I cannot know whether a crowd would prefer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would put a small part of each paid festival fee into savings after the mortgage and food clear. In the first year after 2036 I would compare actual festival and school pay, and apply for a qualified school aide opening only if both incomes fall short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant stage work, but our four-month cushion and current pay make the next few years manageable. I still want a bigger reserve before any switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if festival invitations do not pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count an unpaid festival invitation in the savings plan. If paid dates fall, I would protect two months of expenses while looking for a school role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that a union can ask for fair terms, but each of us still has to practise. I want them to see both parts of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording fees could go before I qualify for paid school work. Written festival dates, wage help during a gap and a school opening that accepts my education would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets a paid hour to train the next teacher. A child cannot learn from a volunteer who has gone to another shift.

headlineQuote: A child cannot learn from a volunteer who has gone to another shift.
portrait: At **43**, Hana is a junior saxophonist with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and four months saved.
Her partner’s **school office pay** steadies the household while festival and recording fees remain uncertain.
She uses **AI daily** for practice sheets but tests new range tools only with trusted demonstration and manual checks.
She asks the **association** for paid training and wage help, seeking school work only when qualified and pickup fits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may end recording fees before Hana qualifies for paid school work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written festival dates**, gap income help and a school opening accepting her education would let her keep earning.
